body: {"total":5,"records":[{"title":"Pre-hospital tranexamic acid in a rural ambulance service: eligibility, administration and delays in a retrospective records review","authors":"MacAlister-Oyebanji R, Thorsby-Nwankwo E","year":2020,"venue":"Rural Emergency Care Journal","doi":"10.5555/recj.2020.0271","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed electronic patient care records for 612 adults who met a rural ambulance service's criteria for tranexamic acid after injury over three years. Fifty-eight percent received tranexamic acid before hospital arrival, at a median of 52 minutes after injury. Administration was less common when a single paramedic attended (41 percent) and for patients aged over 65 (49 percent). Eleven percent of those treated received the drug more than three hours after injury, against the protocol. Records did not always state the time of injury, which was estimated for 18 percent of patients. Hospital outcomes were not available."},{"title":"Timing of tranexamic acid after injury and death from bleeding: a systematic review of individual patient data","authors":"Oduya-Brennan K, Lefevre-Mahlangu T, Ishikawa-Doherty P","year":2018,"venue":"Trauma and Resuscitation Reviews","doi":"10.5555/trr.2018.0114","providerType":"review","abstract":"We pooled individual data on 38,900 bleeding patients from randomised trials of tranexamic acid. Immediate treatment reduced the odds of death from bleeding by about 70 percent, and the benefit fell by about 10 percent for every 15 minutes of delay, with no benefit seen after three hours. There was no increase in vascular occlusive events overall. Most participants were treated in hospital, and few trials recorded the time of pre-hospital administration, so the effect of delays before arrival is inferred from in-hospital timing."},{"title":"Linking ambulance and hospital records for trauma outcome audit: matching rates and pitfalls","authors":"Venter-Gallagher S, Okonkwo-Laine J","year":2022,"venue":"Emergency Services Informatics","doi":"10.5555/esi.2022.0053","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We linked ambulance patient care records to emergency department and inpatient records in one region using date of birth, sex, postcode and arrival time. Linkage matched 91 percent of trauma patients conveyed directly but only 78 percent of those transferred between hospitals, and matching was lower for patients with missing identifiers at the scene. Unmatched patients were more often older, more severely injured and transferred. The authors warn that outcome audits based on linked data will overrepresent less severely injured patients unless unmatched records are followed up by hand, which requires a data-sharing agreement covering all sites."},{"title":"Thromboembolic events after pre-hospital tranexamic acid in older trauma patients: a registry analysis","authors":"Pellegrini-Achterberg M, Sato-Okafor L, Dunmore-Reyes A","year":2024,"venue":"Geriatric Trauma Research","doi":"10.5555/gtr.2024.0190","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using a regional trauma registry, we compared 1,020 patients aged 65 or over who received pre-hospital tranexamic acid with 1,540 who did not. Venous thromboembolism within 30 days was recorded in 3.1 and 2.4 percent respectively (adjusted odds ratio 1.21, 95 percent CI 0.78 to 1.88). Mortality did not differ after adjustment for injury severity and anticoagulant use. Treated patients were more severely injured, and the registry captured only patients admitted to trauma units, so the analysis may miss events after discharge or among patients managed in smaller hospitals."},{"title":"Why paramedics withhold tranexamic acid in rural trauma: a qualitative study of decision-making","authors":"Hollis-Adebayo K, Strand-Mwangi P","year":2023,"venue":"Prehospital Care Research","doi":"10.5555/pcr.2023.0158","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 24 paramedics from two rural ambulance services about recent trauma calls in which tranexamic acid was or was not given. Paramedics described three main reasons for withholding it: uncertainty about the time of injury, the workload of a single-crew response while managing the airway and bleeding, and worry about giving it to older patients taking anticoagulants. Several said they would give it more readily with a checklist prompt on the electronic patient care record. Paramedics rarely learned what happened to their patients after handover, which they felt made it hard to judge whether their decisions were right."}]}
